claim: Telomere length distributions contain a fingerprint of progressive telomere loss and the fraction of symmetric cell proliferations.
source: Our mathematical model shows that these distributions contain a fingerprint of the progressive telomere loss and the fraction of symmetric cell proliferations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mathematical model developed in the study and tested against measured data.

claim: The study analyzed telomere length distributions from 356 healthy individuals, including 47 cord blood and 28 bone marrow samples.
source: Our predictions are tested against measured telomere length distributions in humans across all ages, collected from lymphocyte and granulocyte sorted telomere length data of 356 healthy individuals, including 47 cord blood and 28 bone marrow samples.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection in the study.

claim: There is an increasing stem cell pool during childhood and adolescence.
source: We find an increasing stem cell pool during childhood and adolescence and an approximately maintained stem cell population in adults.
evidence: This finding is derived from analysis of telomere length data across different age groups.

claim: The stem cell population is approximately maintained in adults.
source: We find an increasing stem cell pool during childhood and adolescence and an approximately maintained stem cell population in adults.
evidence: This finding is derived from analysis of telomere length data in adult populations.

claim: The method can detect individual differences from a single tissue sample.
source: Furthermore, our method is able to detect individual differences from a single tissue sample, i.e. a single snapshot.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mathematical model and individual sample analyses presented in the study.

claim: Homeostasis in most mammalian tissues is maintained by occasional differentiation of infrequently dividing multi-potent stem cells.
source: Homeostasis is in most mammalian tissues maintained by the occasional differentiation of infrequently dividing multi-potent stem cells (Li and Clevers, 2010; Busch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Stem cells are involved in the formation, maintenance, renewal, and aging of tissues.
source: These cells are involved in the formation, maintenance, renewal, and aging of tissues (Reya et al., 2001; Morrison and Kimble, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The longevity of stem cells imposes the risk of accumulation of multiple mutations that can cause cancer.
source: Their longevity imposes the risk of the accumulation of multiple mutations that potentially induce aberrant stem cell proliferation and can ultimately cause the emergence of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on cancer biology.

claim: Telomeres are noncoding repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of all eukaryotic chromosomes.
source: Telomeres are noncoding repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of all eukaryotic chromosomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about telomere structure.

claim: In vertebrates, telomere sequences consist of hundreds to thousands of repeats of the nucleobase blocks TTAGGG.
source: In vertebrates, these sequences consist of hundreds to thousands of repeats of the nucleobase blocks TTAGGG (Griffith et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Telomere repeats are progressively lost in most somatic cells with age.
source: Telomere repeats are progressively lost in most somatic cells with age, as the conventional DNA polymerase is unable to fully copy the lagging DNA strand of chromosomes during cell replication (Olovnikov, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on the end-replication problem.

claim: Short telomeres are associated with genetic instability.
source: Short telomeres are associated with genetic instability (Hande, 1999; Feldser et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Short telomeres trigger DNA-damage checkpoint pathways and enforce permanent cell cycle arrest.
source: They trigger DNA-damage checkpoint pathways and enforce permanent cell cycle arrest ( d'Adda di Fagagna et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Telomere length limits the replication capacity of somatic cells.
source: Thus, telomere length limits the replication capacity of somatic cells (Hayflick and Moorhead, 1961) and can indirectly act as a tumor suppressor (Kinzler and Vogelstein, 1997; Campisi, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research including the Hayflick limit.

claim: Telomerase is an enzyme that tags additional TTAGGG repeats to the end of chromosomes by utilizing single stranded RNA templates.
source: This effect can be attenuated by the enzyme telomerase, which tags additional TTAGGG repeats to the end of chromosomes by utilizing single stranded RNA templates (Greider and Blackburn, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the foundational research on telomerase.

claim: Telomerase is primarily expressed in compartments of stem and germ line cells, as well as in numerous tumors.
source: Telomerase is primarily expressed in compartments of stem and germ line cells, as well as in numerous tumors (Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Telomerase expression levels are insufficient to prevent the progressive loss of telomere repeats in most healthy human tissues with age.
source: However, telomerase expression levels are insufficient to prevent the progressive loss of telomere repeats in most healthy human tissues with age (Harley et al., 1990; Rufer et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Healthy human cells contain 184 telomeres, four on each of the 46 chromosomes.
source: Healthy human cells contain 184 telomeres, four on each of the 46 chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human cell biology.

claim: The average telomere length of a cell shortens by a constant factor during each division.
source: Thus, the average telomere length of a cell shortens by a constant factor during each division.
evidence: This is an assumption of the mathematical model based on established knowledge.

claim: It is the length of the shortest telomere rather than the average telomere length that triggers cell cycle arrest.
source: Such an approach might underestimate the number of senescent cells once telomeres become critically short, since it is the length of the shortest telomere rather then the average telomere length that triggers cell cycle arrest (Hemann et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: All non-hematopoietic stem cells will eventually be depleted without continuous stem cell turnover.
source: Although some of the progeny, particularly primitive progenitor cells, can be long lived and are able to maintain homeostasis without stem cell turnover for intermediate time intervals, eventually all non hematopoietic stem cells will be depleted without continuous stem cell turn over (Busch et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cells leaving the stem cell pool have an approximately constant number of cell divisions before they reach maturation.
source: Cells leaving the stem cell pool have an approximately constant number of cell divisions before they reach maturation (Takano, 2004; Werner et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The distribution of telomere lengths of mature cells is a good proxy for the distribution of telomere lengths in stem cells.
source: This shifts the distribution to shorter values of telomere length and consequently, the distribution of telomere lengths of mature cells is a good proxy for the distribution of telomere lengths in stem cells (Rodriguez-Brenes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and is a key assumption of the model.

claim: The expected telomere length distribution becomes a traveling wave that starts narrowly distributed around an initial telomere length and shifts towards shorter average telomere length with time.
source: It becomes a traveling wave that starts narrowly distributed around an initial telomere length and shifts towards shorter average telomere length with time.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model.

claim: Under the presence of symmetric stem cell self-renewal, the telomere length follows a logarithmic decay with age.
source: We find that the telomere length follows a logarithmic decay with age (see also Equation S19), given by
evidence: This is a mathematical prediction from model 2.

claim: Telomere length was measured in lymphocytes and granulocytes in a cohort of 356 healthy humans with ages between 0 and 85 years.
source: In order to test the predictions of our model experimentally, we have measured telomere length in lymphocytes and granulocytes in a cohort of 356 healthy humans with ages between 0 and 85 years.
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection.

claim: The data includes 47 cord blood samples of healthy children and bone marrow biopsies of 28 patients with diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma without bone marrow involvement.
source: Our data includes 47 cord blood samples of healthy children and bone marrow biopsies of 28 patients with diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma without bone marrow involvement.
evidence: This describes the composition of the experimental data set.

claim: Average telomere length in all 356 samples was assessed with established Flow-FISH protocols.
source: We assessed the average telomere length in all 356 samples with established Flow-FISH protocols (Aubert et al., 2012; Baerlocher et al., 2006; Weidner et al., 2014; Beier et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology with citations to established protocols.

claim: 28 blood samples of lymphocytes, 10 blood samples of granulocytes and 28 bone marrow biopsies were analyzed with quantitative-fluorescence in situ hybridisation (Q-FISH).
source: In addition, we have analyzed 28 blood samples of lymphocytes, 10 blood samples of granulocytes and 28 bone marrow biopsies with quantitative-fluorescence in situ hybridisation (Q-FISH) (Beier et al., 2015; Varela et al., 2011; Zijlmans et al., 1997)
evidence: This describes additional experimental data collection with citations to methods.

claim: If a cell loses on average 50 bp telomeric repeats per cell division, this implies approximately 1 replication per year for hematopoietic stem cells.
source: If for example a cell looses on average 50 bp telomeric repeats per cell division (Rufer et al., 1999), this implies approximately 1 replication per year for the hematopoietic stem cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the data combined with cited knowledge about telomere loss per division.

claim: The assumption of strictly asymmetric cell divisions (model 1) fails to explain the pronounced loss of telomere repeats in infants.
source: However, the assumption of strictly asymmetric cell divisions (model 1) fails to explain the pronounced loss of telomere repeats in infants (prediction of model 1 for the initial telomere length in lymphocytes: 9.8±0.15 kbp, measured average initial telomere length: 10.67±0.4 kbp, similar results for granulocytes, see also Figure 4 for a comparison of model 1 and model 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claim: For lymphocytes, the parameter controlling average loss of telomere length is 75±7 bp/year, initial telomere length is 10.4±0.2 kbp, and probability for symmetric stem cell self-renewal is 0.35 ± 0.07.
source: Maximum likelihood estimates of our general mathematical solution (Equation 4) to the telomere length data on the population level (see Figure 3) reveals for the parameter controlling average loss of telomere length in lymphocytes a value of 75±7 bp/year, an initial telomere length of 10.4±0.2 kbp and a probability for symmetric stem cell self-renewal of 0.35 ± 0.07.
evidence: These are parameter estimates from fitting model 2 to experimental data.

claim: For granulocytes, the telomere loss is 68±5 bp/year, initial telomere length is 10.2±0.3 kbp, and probability for symmetric stem cell self-renewal is 0.44 ± 0.2.
source: In granulocytes we find a value of telomere loss of 68±5 bp/year, an initial telomere length of 10.2±0.3 kbp and a probability for symmetric stem cell self-renewal of 0.44 ± 0.2.
evidence: These are parameter estimates from fitting model 2 to experimental data.

claim: An independent data set of 835 healthy humans confirms the parameter estimations, particularly the accelerated decrease of average telomere length during adolescence.
source: In addition to our group of 356 healthy humans, we have tested our hypothesis in an independent data set of 835 healthy humans, previously published by an unrelated group in (Aubert et al., 2012), see Figure 3—figure supplement 1. This set confirms our parameter estimations, in particular the accelerated decrease of average telomere length during adolescence is also observed.
evidence: This describes validation of findings using an independent dataset.

claim: The increased loss of telomere repeats in the first years of human life is a consequence of an expanding stem cell population.
source: Our model suggests that the increased loss of telomere repeats in the first years of human life is a consequence of an expanding stem cell population.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the mathematical model.

claim: Approximately 70% of stem cell divisions are asymmetric and 30% are symmetric self-renewals.
source: We find approximately 70% of stem cell divisions are asymmetric and 30% are symmetric self-renewals.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian inference analysis of the data.

claim: There is a transition in stem cell dynamics between the 6th and 7th year of life for lymphocytes.
source: This approach suggests at most two separate phases, with a transition between the 6th and 7th year of life for lymphocytes, see Figure 5f–i, and a transition between the 10th and 15th years of life for granulocytes, see Figure 5j–m.
evidence: This is a finding from the multi-phase Bayesian analysis.

claim: There is a transition in stem cell dynamics between the 10th and 15th years of life for granulocytes.
source: This approach suggests at most two separate phases, with a transition between the 6th and 7th year of life for lymphocytes, see Figure 5f–i, and a transition between the 10th and 15th years of life for granulocytes, see Figure 5j–m.
evidence: This is a finding from the multi-phase Bayesian analysis.

claim: The probability of symmetric stem cell self-renewal in adults is in the range of p∈(0,0.2).
source: The probability of symmetric stem cell self-renewal in adults however is in the the range of p∈(0,0.2).
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian analysis of adult data.

claim: Model 2 (with symmetric and asymmetric divisions) is the best explanation for the observed data based on Akaike information criterion.
source: Model 1 scores with an AIC of 2550, model 2 has an AIC of 2328 and a multiphase model with a minimum of 7 parameters yields an AIC of 2361. The AIC is minimized by model 2.
evidence: This is a result from statistical model selection analysis.

claim: A low probability of symmetric self-renewal (p between 0.005 to 0.03 per cell division) was found in all individual samples.
source: We find a low probability of symmetric self-renewal (p between 0.005 to 0.03 per cell division) in all individual samples.
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the model to individual telomere length distributions.

claim: The average telomere loss per year varies between individuals and ranges from 18 bp/year to 110 bp/year.
source: Also the average telomere loss per year varies between individuals and ranges from 18 bp/year to 110 bp/year.
evidence: This is a finding from individual sample analysis.

claim: The loss of telomeric repeats slows down with age in granulocytes.
source: We find differences between individual samples of lymphocytes and granulocytes. While the loss of telomeric repeats slows down with age in granulocytes, it slightly accelerates in lymphocytes, see Figure 7.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of individual samples shown in Figure 7.

claim: The loss of telomeric repeats slightly accelerates with age in lymphocytes.
source: We find differences between individual samples of lymphocytes and granulocytes. While the loss of telomeric repeats slows down with age in granulocytes, it slightly accelerates in lymphocytes, see Figure 7.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of individual samples shown in Figure 7.

claim: The reduced rate of telomere loss in granulocytes is in agreement with a skewed differentiation potential towards the myeloid lineage of aged hematopoietic stem cells.
source: In our model, such a reduced rate of telomere loss can be explained with an increased reservoir of myeloid specific stem and progenitor cells and is in agreement with a skewed differentiation potential towards the myeloid lineage of aged hematopoietic stem cells (Geiger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The rate of telomere loss decreases with age in granulocytes at -0.78 bp/year.
source: The rate of telomere loss decreases with age in granulocytes (−0.78 bp/year, dark red line)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The rate of telomere loss increases with age in lymphocytes at +0.27 bp/year.
source: but increases in lymphocytes (+0.27 bp/year, dark green dashed line)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The rate of telomere loss in bone marrow sections decreases with age at -0.36 bp/year.
source: The rate of telomere loss decreases with age in granulocytes (−0.78 bp/year, dark red line) and in bone marrow sections (−0.36 bp/year, grey dotted line)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Peripheral blood of 309 healthy blood donors was obtained from the blood donor bank in Aachen.
source: Peripheral blood of 309 healthy blood donors was obtained from the blood donor bank in Aachen.
evidence: This describes the source of experimental samples.

claim: Q-FISH of peripheral blood cytospins was performed on 28 healthy blood samples.
source: Q-FISH of peripheral blood cytospins was performed on 28 healthy blood samples.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology applied to a subset of samples.

claim: 47 cord blood and blood samples from healthy children and adolescents were obtained from the Department of Pediatrics and Neonatology of the University Hospital of Aachen.
source: 47 cord blood and blood samples from healthy children and adolescents were obtained from the Department of Pediatrics and Neonatology of the University Hospital of Aachen.
evidence: This describes the source of pediatric samples.

claim: Bone marrow biopsies of 28 patients with diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma without bone marrow involvement were used for bone marrow analysis.
source: Bone marrow biopsies of 28 patients with diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma without bone marrow involvement were used for bone marrow analysis.
evidence: This describes the source of bone marrow samples used as healthy controls.

claim: All samples were taken with informed consent and according to the guidelines of the ethics committees at University Hospital Aachen.
source: All samples were taken with informed consent and according to the guidelines of the ethics committees at University Hospital Aachen.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.
